screens.title: Introduction to Amazon EC2
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore Amazon EC2 — Elastic Compute Cloud — the AWS service that provides virtual servers you can rent and control. Think of EC2 as a computer you can start and stop on demand. It gives you an instance, which runs an operating system and your applications, without buying physical hardware. We’ll explain the building blocks: AMIs, which are templates that include an operating system and software; instance types, which define C P U, memory and networking; key pairs, used for secure administrative access; and security groups, which act as virtual firewalls. You’ll also follow the conceptual steps for launching and connecting to an instance and see a short scenario for a web server. Understanding EC2 is crucial because it’s the foundation for running many workloads in AWS — from simple websites to data processing clusters. Notice how the components work together: an AMI gives you a starting image, an instance type gives you capacity, key pairs secure access, and security groups protect network traffic. By the end you’ll be able to identify each piece and why it matters when you design or operate cloud systems.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Introduction to Amazon EC2
Introduction to Amazon EC2
Elastic Compute Cloud: rent virtual servers that scale with demand
What EC2 provides
Resizable virtual servers called instances, configurable with AMIs and instance types so you pay only for what you use.
Security basics
Key pairs for admin access and security groups as instance-level firewalls. Follow least privilege when opening ports.
Why it matters
EC2 underpins many architectures. Choosing the right AMI and instance type controls cost and performance.
Explore Key Topics
AMI
Pre-configured template containing an OS and software to launch instances consistently.
Instance type
Defines CPU, memory and networking; pick a family optimized for your workload.
Security
Key pairs for secure access, security groups to control traffic and reduce exposure.
EC2 Concept Map
AMI
Template with OS and apps
Creates consistent instances
Instance Type
Defines CPU, memory, network
Family choices for workload fit
Security
Key pairs and security groups
Protect access and traffic
Quick scenario
An Amazon Linux 2 AMI plus a t2.micro instance type can host a small web server. You’d generate a key pair, configure a security group to permit HTTP and SSH from trusted IPs, then launch and connect via SSH using your private key.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what Amazon EC2 is and why 'elastic' matters, identify the main EC2 building blocks — instances, AMIs, instance types, key pairs and security groups — and describe their roles. You will also understand the step-by-step process to launch an instance and how to connect to Linux instances securely. Finally, you will be able to recognize common EC2 use cases such as hosting web servers and small development environments, and identify frequent configuration mistakes such as overly permissive security group rules or losing a private key. These objectives are practical: in a conceptual hands-on activity you will select an Amazon Linux 2 AMI, pick a small instance type, generate and secure a key pair, model security group rules that permit only the necessary traffic, and prepare an SSH connection string. Knowing these objectives helps you focus on the decisions that affect cost, performance, and security in cloud deployments. Each objective links a concept to a small, verifiable competency so you can measure your readiness.

screens.title: What is an EC2 Instance?
screens.narratorSegment: An EC2 instance is a virtual server running in AWS that you can start, stop, and configure like a physical machine. It runs an operating system and your applications, and you control its size and network access. The idea is simple: instead of buying hardware, you rent compute capacity. This allows teams to provision exact resources they need and only pay for usage. For example, a small web application can run on a t2. micro instance, while a compute-heavy batch job might run on a compute-optimized instance. A common misconception is that an instance is just a container or a lightweight process; it behaves more like a full virtual machine with its own OS and network identity. Another important point is that instances are ephemeral by default — their root storage may not persist if you use instance store volumes, so persistent storage is typically provided with attached volumes. A concrete example: you launch an instance from an Amazon Linux 2 AMI, install a web server, and configure a security group to allow HTTP. The key takeaway is that an instance is your cloud-based server: you choose its image, size, and security, and those choices determine performance, cost, and accessibility. Which instance would you pick when you expect unpredictable traffic patterns?

keyIdea.text: An EC2 instance is a cloud virtual server with an OS and apps that you configure, scale, and secure for your workload.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is an EC2 Instance?
Definition
EC2 instance
A virtual server in AWS that runs an operating system and your applications and can be started, stopped, and resized.
Analogy
Think of an instance as a rented virtual computer. You select its template and resources, similar to choosing a laptop model and preinstalled software.
Key Takeaway
Instances act like full virtual machines: they carry OS, apps, identity, and network access, and decisions affect cost and performance.
Primary teaching area
Behavior
  • Runs a full OS and applications.
  • Has a network identity and IP address.
  • Can be resized or replaced as demand changes.
Common uses
  • Web servers, application servers, dev environments.
  • Batch processing and ephemeral compute tasks.
  • Part of larger architectures behind load balancers.
Concrete example
Launch Amazon Linux 2, install a web server, and allow HTTP traffic in a security group. The instance serves web pages and can be stopped to avoid charges when idle.

screens.title: Amazon Machine Image (AMI)
screens.narratorSegment: An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is a pre-configured template that contains an operating system and optional software used to launch EC2 instances. When you pick an AMI you choose the starting point for your server: the OS, language runtime, and any included packages. AWS offers public AMIs such as Amazon Linux 2 and other community or marketplace AMIs, and you can create a custom AMI from an existing instance to capture a configured state for repeatable deployments. A useful example is creating a custom AMI for a web server image that already has your application and dependencies installed. This ensures new instances launch in a known state. A common misconception is that AMIs are only OS images. In fact they can include application and configuration layers, which is why teams use AMIs to standardize deployments. When designing AMIs, think about upkeep: custom AMIs should be versioned and updated to include security patches. The core takeaway is that AMIs are cookie cutters: they let you launch many consistent servers quickly, which simplifies scaling and reduces configuration drift. How would you version and update a custom AMI for a production web service?

keyIdea.title: AMI purpose
keyIdea.text: An AMI is a template containing OS and optional software; use custom AMIs to standardize and speed up instance launches.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Amazon Machine Image (AMI)
What is an AMI?
Pre-configured instance template
Contains an OS and optional application components so new instances start in a known state.
When to create one
Create custom AMIs after configuring an instance to include application code and dependencies for repeatable deployments.
Key Takeaway
Use AMIs to standardize instance creation and reduce setup time when scaling or replacing servers.
AMI examples and notes
Public AMI
Provided by AWS, e.g., Amazon Linux 2, ready for general use.
Custom AMI
Created from a configured instance to capture software, settings and optimizations.
Maintenance
Version and update AMIs to include patches; avoid running long-lived unpatched images in production.
Concrete example
Create a custom AMI from a web server with application code preinstalled. Launch new instances from that AMI to scale horizontally with identical configuration.

screens.title: Instance Types: Choosing Capacity
screens.narratorSegment: Instance types define the virtual hardware for your EC2 instance: the number of virtual CPUs, memory size, storage options, and network capacity. AWS groups instance types into families optimized for different workloads: general purpose families balance C P U and memory for broad use, compute optimized families prioritize C P U for heavy computations, memory optimized families provide extra R A M for large in-memory workloads, and storage optimized families focus on high input and output for disk-heavy tasks. Choosing the right instance type is a trade-off: pick too small and performance suffers; pick too large and costs rise unnecessarily. For example, a t2. micro is often sufficient for small, low-traffic web servers or development instances, while a c5 family instance is better for compute-intensive batch processing. A common misconception is that the largest instance always yields better value; in reality right-sizing matters and horizontal scaling can be more cost-effective than a single large instance. To select an instance type, start with workload profiling — estimate C P U and memory needs — then choose a family and size that meet performance targets while minimizing cost. The takeaway is to match workload characteristics to the instance family and consider scaling patterns as part of the decision.

keyIdea.title: Instance types
keyIdea.text: Pick a family and size that match CPU, memory, and storage needs; avoid defaulting to the largest instance and practice right-sizing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Instance Types
Instance type families
Compare capacity trade-offs to choose the best fit
General purpose
Balanced CPU and memory for a wide range of workloads, useful for small web servers and microservices.
Compute optimized
High CPU performance for batch processing or compute-bound tasks.
Memory optimized
Extra RAM for in-memory databases and analytics workloads.
Concrete example
A t2.micro is suitable for a low-traffic website because it provides a small amount of CPU and memory at low cost. For a CPU-heavy worker you would consider a compute-optimized instance that gives better throughput per dollar for that workload.
Misconception
Bigger always better is false. Oversizing costs more and may not improve throughput if the workload is I/O bound or limited by other resources.
Pro tip
Profile actual CPU and memory usage before choosing a production instance type. Consider horizontal scaling as an efficient alternative to a single large instance.

screens.title: Key Pairs: Secure Administrative Access
screens.narratorSegment: Key pairs are cryptographic credentials used to access EC2 instances securely. A key pair consists of a public key that AWS stores and a private key file that you download and keep safe, typically with a. pem extension. When you launch an instance you associate a key pair with it; that public key is placed on the instance so your private key can authenticate you over SSH. For Linux instances, you use SSH with your private key to gain shell access. A concrete example: after generating a key pair named my-webserver-key, you store my-webserver-key. pem locally and apply strict file permissions. Then you use an SSH client to authenticate to the instance. A common mistake is losing the private key — if that happens you cannot SSH into the instance and must follow recovery procedures like creating a new instance or using cloud console methods. Another mistake is exposing the private key or leaving open SSH access to the internet. The core takeaway is to generate keys carefully, protect the private key, set correct file permissions, and limit SSH access through security group rules. How will you store and back up your private keys securely in practice?

keyIdea.title: Key pair role
keyIdea.text: A key pair provides SSH authentication: AWS holds the public key; you keep the private key and use it to connect securely to instances.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Pairs
What is a key pair?
Cryptographic public/private keys used for secure SSH access to instances.
Process
  1. Generate key pair in console or tool.
  2. Download private key (.pem) and keep it secure.
  3. Associate the key with the instance at launch.
Concrete example
Generate my-webserver-key, store my-webserver-key.pem locally with strict permissions, and use it with SSH to connect to your Linux instance.
Common mistakes
Losing the private key prevents SSH access; sharing or exposing the private key allows unauthorized access.
Warning
Never leave SSH open to the world and never store private keys in public locations.
Takeaway
Key pairs are central to secure instance management. Protect the private key and control SSH access via security groups.

screens.title: Security Groups: Virtual Firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. You define rules that permit traffic by protocol, port range and source or destination. For example, to allow a web server to receive traffic you add inbound rules that permit TCP on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. For administrative access you typically allow SSH on port 22 from a specific IP address. A common beginner mistake is to open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0, which allows anyone on the internet to attempt connections and increases risk. Security groups are stateful: if you allow an inbound connection, the response traffic is permitted automatically. Another misconception is treating security groups like operating-system firewalls; they are complementary but operate at the cloud network level. Concrete example: create a security group allowing TCP 80 and 443 from anywhere for a public web server, and allow TCP 22 only from your home IP for SSH. The core takeaway is to follow the principle of least privilege — only open the ports and IP ranges necessary, and review rules regularly. How would you audit security group rules for unnecessary exposure?

How would you audit security group rules for unnecessary exposure?

keyIdea.title: Security group principle
keyIdea.text: Use security groups to restrict traffic to required ports and sources; avoid broad rules like SSH open to all.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Security Groups
Security groups as virtual firewalls
Define inbound and outbound rules to control traffic at the instance level
Inbound rules example
HTTP: TCP 80, Source: 0.0.0.0/0 (if public web). HTTPS: TCP 443, Source: 0.0.0.0/0. SSH: TCP 22, Source: your IP (e.g., 203.0.113.42/32).
Stateful behavior
Security groups are stateful: responses to allowed inbound traffic are permitted automatically without explicit outbound rules for the same connection.
Pro tip
Limit SSH to known IP ranges and use separate security groups for different roles — web servers, databases, and management instances.
Concrete scenario
For a public web server: allow TCP 80 and 443 from anywhere, but restrict SSH (TCP 22) to your office or home IP address only. This prevents broad exposure to SSH attacks.

screens.title: Launching an EC2 Instance — Step by Step
screens.narratorSegment: Launching an EC2 instance follows a clear sequence of decisions and configurations. Start by choosing an AMI, which defines the operating system and any preinstalled software. Next pick an instance type to set C P U, memory, and network capacity. Then configure instance details like the number of instances, network placement, and IAM role if the instance needs permissions. Add storage volumes as required — persistent volumes are covered in the next chapter but remember to plan for persistent data. Add tags to organize resources, and then configure a security group to permit the traffic your workload needs. Finally, review settings and launch the instance while associating a key pair for administrative access. A concrete example: choose Amazon Linux 2 AMI, select t2. micro for a small server, set a single instance in the selected VPC and subnet, add an EBS volume for the root device, tag with Name:web-server, create a security group allowing HTTP and SSH from your IP, then launch using a new key pair. A common misconception is that all decisions must be perfect the first time; you can stop an instance, modify settings, or create new AMIs and relaunch. The takeaway is that launching is a repeatable sequence: AMI → instance type → configuration → storage → tags → security → key pair → launch. Which step would you check carefully to ensure security?

keyIdea.title: Launch sequence
keyIdea.text: Follow the repeated steps: choose AMI, select instance type, configure, add storage and tags, set security, attach key pair, then launch.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Launching an EC2 Instance
Launch sequence
A repeatable set of steps to start a running instance
Step 1
Choose an AMI (e.g., Amazon Linux 2).
Step 2
Select an instance type (t2.micro for small workloads).
Step 3
Configure details: count, network, IAM role.
Step 4
Add storage volumes (EBS) for persistence.
Step 5
Add tags for organization and identification.
Step 6
Configure a security group to permit required traffic.
Concrete example
Pick Amazon Linux 2, t2.micro, single instance, add an EBS root volume, tag Name:web-server, add inbound rules for HTTP and SSH from your IP, then launch with a new key pair.

screens.title: Connecting to a Linux EC2 Instance via SSH
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting to a Linux EC2 instance uses SSH with the private key of the key pair you associated at launch. Before connecting, ensure the private key file has strict permissions so SSH will accept it. For example, set the file to read-only for the owner. Use the default username for the AMI — for Amazon Linux 2 that is ec2-user, while other AMIs may use ubuntu or a different account. The visual code panel shows an example SSH command you would run from a terminal, using your private key and the instance’s public DNS name. A frequent beginner mistake is pasting the private key into a shared location or leaving SSH open to all IPs; instead, keep the key local and limit security group SSH access to a trusted IP. If you cannot connect, check that the instance has a public IP or an appropriate public subnet, the security group permits SSH from your source, and the username matches the AMI. The takeaway: prepare file permissions, confirm security group rules and the username, then run the SSH command. If connection still fails, review both key placement and network settings.

keyIdea.title: SSH prep

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Connect via SSH
SSH connection checklist
Prepare key permissions and confirm network access
Checklist
  • Private key (.pem) is stored locally and permissioned (read-only for owner).
  • Security group allows SSH from your source IP.
  • Instance has a public IP or an accessible network path.
  • Username matches the AMI (ec2-user for Amazon Linux 2).
Common error
Permissions too open on the private key will prevent SSH from using it; adjust permissions before connecting.
Terminal example

Concrete note
Do not share the .pem file. Use strict file permissions and restrict SSH access in the security group to trusted IPs.

screens.title: Common EC2 Use Cases and Architectures
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 instances are versatile building blocks in many architectures. For a simple web application, an instance can run a web server behind a load balancer; you might scale horizontally by running multiple instances from the same AMI, with an Auto Scaling group added later. For development, a single lightweight instance is often enough. In data processing, clusters of compute-optimized instances handle batch jobs or analytics. A misconception is that EC2 must be used alone; in practice it often integrates with other services like load balancers, storage volumes, and managed databases. Consider a three-tier architecture: web servers on EC2 instances in the front tier, application servers in the middle, and a managed database for persistence. EC2 provides the compute layer and is typically paired with EBS for storage. For small workloads you might run a single instance with an attached volume; for fault tolerance you run multiple instances across availability zones. The takeaway is that EC2 fits many roles — from a single web server to a horizontally scaled fleet — and should be combined with other services to meet availability and scaling goals. Which architecture would you pick for a high-availability web app?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore Amazon EC2 — Elastic Compute Cloud — the AWS service that provides virtual servers you can rent and control. Think of EC2 as a computer you can start and stop on demand. It gives you an instance, which runs an operating system and your applications, without buying physical hardware. We’ll explain the building blocks: AMIs, which are templates that include an operating system and software; instance types, which define C P U, memory and networking; key pairs, used for secure administrative access; and security groups, which act as virtual firewalls. You’ll also follow the conceptual steps for launching and connecting to an instance and see a short scenario for a web server. Understanding EC2 is crucial because it’s the foundation for running many workloads in AWS — from simple websites to data processing clusters. Notice how the components work together: an AMI gives you a starting image, an instance type gives you capacity, key pairs secure access, and security groups protect network traffic. By the end you’ll be able to identify each piece and why it matters when you design or operate cloud systems.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what Amazon EC2 is and why 'elastic' matters, identify the main EC2 building blocks — instances, AMIs, instance types, key pairs and security groups — and describe their roles. You will also understand the step-by-step process to launch an instance and how to connect to Linux instances securely. Finally, you will be able to recognize common EC2 use cases such as hosting web servers and small development environments, and identify frequent configuration mistakes such as overly permissive security group rules or losing a private key. These objectives are practical: in a conceptual hands-on activity you will select an Amazon Linux 2 AMI, pick a small instance type, generate and secure a key pair, model security group rules that permit only the necessary traffic, and prepare an SSH connection string. Knowing these objectives helps you focus on the decisions that affect cost, performance, and security in cloud deployments. Each objective links a concept to a small, verifiable competency so you can measure your readiness.

These objectives focus on actionable skills. You will learn to choose an AMI for a workload, pick an instance type that balances cost and capacity, generate and safeguard a key pair, and craft security group rules that follow least privilege. For example, practice selecting an Amazon Linux 2 AMI to host a small web server, choose a t2. micro for low-traffic sites, create a. pem private key and restrict its file permissions, and add inbound rules only from your IP for SSH while allowing HTTP and HTTPS from appropriate sources. These exercises build muscle memory for real cloud tasks and help you avoid common errors, such as opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 or forgetting to protect the private key. Each objective pairs a concept (like AMI or security group) with why it matters in deployment, so you can measure readiness by performing the conceptual hands-on steps in a simulated activity. This prepares you for later chapters that add storage and networking detail.

An EC2 instance is a virtual server running in AWS that you can start, stop, and configure like a physical machine. It runs an operating system and your applications, and you control its size and network access. The idea is simple: instead of buying hardware, you rent compute capacity. This allows teams to provision exact resources they need and only pay for usage. For example, a small web application can run on a t2. micro instance, while a compute-heavy batch job might run on a compute-optimized instance. A common misconception is that an instance is just a container or a lightweight process; it behaves more like a full virtual machine with its own OS and network identity. Another important point is that instances are ephemeral by default — their root storage may not persist if you use instance store volumes, so persistent storage is typically provided with attached volumes. A concrete example: you launch an instance from an Amazon Linux 2 AMI, install a web server, and configure a security group to allow HTTP. The key takeaway is that an instance is your cloud-based server: you choose its image, size, and security, and those choices determine performance, cost, and accessibility. Which instance would you pick when you expect unpredictable traffic patterns?

An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is a pre-configured template that contains an operating system and optional software used to launch EC2 instances. When you pick an AMI you choose the starting point for your server: the OS, language runtime, and any included packages. AWS offers public AMIs such as Amazon Linux 2 and other community or marketplace AMIs, and you can create a custom AMI from an existing instance to capture a configured state for repeatable deployments. A useful example is creating a custom AMI for a web server image that already has your application and dependencies installed. This ensures new instances launch in a known state. A common misconception is that AMIs are only OS images. In fact they can include application and configuration layers, which is why teams use AMIs to standardize deployments. When designing AMIs, think about upkeep: custom AMIs should be versioned and updated to include security patches. The core takeaway is that AMIs are cookie cutters: they let you launch many consistent servers quickly, which simplifies scaling and reduces configuration drift. How would you version and update a custom AMI for a production web service?

Instance types define the virtual hardware for your EC2 instance: the number of virtual CPUs, memory size, storage options, and network capacity. AWS groups instance types into families optimized for different workloads: general purpose families balance C P U and memory for broad use, compute optimized families prioritize C P U for heavy computations, memory optimized families provide extra R A M for large in-memory workloads, and storage optimized families focus on high input and output for disk-heavy tasks. Choosing the right instance type is a trade-off: pick too small and performance suffers; pick too large and costs rise unnecessarily. For example, a t2. micro is often sufficient for small, low-traffic web servers or development instances, while a c5 family instance is better for compute-intensive batch processing. A common misconception is that the largest instance always yields better value; in reality right-sizing matters and horizontal scaling can be more cost-effective than a single large instance. To select an instance type, start with workload profiling — estimate C P U and memory needs — then choose a family and size that meet performance targets while minimizing cost. The takeaway is to match workload characteristics to the instance family and consider scaling patterns as part of the decision.

Key pairs are cryptographic credentials used to access EC2 instances securely. A key pair consists of a public key that AWS stores and a private key file that you download and keep safe, typically with a. pem extension. When you launch an instance you associate a key pair with it; that public key is placed on the instance so your private key can authenticate you over SSH. For Linux instances, you use SSH with your private key to gain shell access. A concrete example: after generating a key pair named my-webserver-key, you store my-webserver-key. pem locally and apply strict file permissions. Then you use an SSH client to authenticate to the instance. A common mistake is losing the private key — if that happens you cannot SSH into the instance and must follow recovery procedures like creating a new instance or using cloud console methods. Another mistake is exposing the private key or leaving open SSH access to the internet. The core takeaway is to generate keys carefully, protect the private key, set correct file permissions, and limit SSH access through security group rules. How will you store and back up your private keys securely in practice?

Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. You define rules that permit traffic by protocol, port range and source or destination. For example, to allow a web server to receive traffic you add inbound rules that permit TCP on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. For administrative access you typically allow SSH on port 22 from a specific IP address. A common beginner mistake is to open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0, which allows anyone on the internet to attempt connections and increases risk. Security groups are stateful: if you allow an inbound connection, the response traffic is permitted automatically. Another misconception is treating security groups like operating-system firewalls; they are complementary but operate at the cloud network level. Concrete example: create a security group allowing TCP 80 and 443 from anywhere for a public web server, and allow TCP 22 only from your home IP for SSH. The core takeaway is to follow the principle of least privilege — only open the ports and IP ranges necessary, and review rules regularly. How would you audit security group rules for unnecessary exposure?

Launching an EC2 instance follows a clear sequence of decisions and configurations. Start by choosing an AMI, which defines the operating system and any preinstalled software. Next pick an instance type to set C P U, memory, and network capacity. Then configure instance details like the number of instances, network placement, and IAM role if the instance needs permissions. Add storage volumes as required — persistent volumes are covered in the next chapter but remember to plan for persistent data. Add tags to organize resources, and then configure a security group to permit the traffic your workload needs. Finally, review settings and launch the instance while associating a key pair for administrative access. A concrete example: choose Amazon Linux 2 AMI, select t2. micro for a small server, set a single instance in the selected VPC and subnet, add an EBS volume for the root device, tag with Name:web-server, create a security group allowing HTTP and SSH from your IP, then launch using a new key pair. A common misconception is that all decisions must be perfect the first time; you can stop an instance, modify settings, or create new AMIs and relaunch. The takeaway is that launching is a repeatable sequence: AMI → instance type → configuration → storage → tags → security → key pair → launch. Which step would you check carefully to ensure security?

Connecting to a Linux EC2 instance uses SSH with the private key of the key pair you associated at launch. Before connecting, ensure the private key file has strict permissions so SSH will accept it. For example, set the file to read-only for the owner. Use the default username for the AMI — for Amazon Linux 2 that is ec2-user, while other AMIs may use ubuntu or a different account. The visual code panel shows an example SSH command you would run from a terminal, using your private key and the instance’s public DNS name. A frequent beginner mistake is pasting the private key into a shared location or leaving SSH open to all IPs; instead, keep the key local and limit security group SSH access to a trusted IP. If you cannot connect, check that the instance has a public IP or an appropriate public subnet, the security group permits SSH from your source, and the username matches the AMI. The takeaway: prepare file permissions, confirm security group rules and the username, then run the SSH command. If connection still fails, review both key placement and network settings.
